title: The Long Dream
author: Zena Hitz
summary: Zena Hitz reflects on lust through Flaubert's Madame Bovary, Chekhov's The Duel, Augustine's Confessions and other literary and philosophical texts. She distinguishes eros, which need not be sexual, from lust, the misuse of sexual desire, and uses Augustine's concept of concupiscence to describe the trap of fixating on pleasure itself rather than its object. Emma Bovary and her seducer treat desire as entertainment, a play in an inner theater, but Hitz notes that tenderness can break through when two people truly see one another, as in Chekhov. She argues that morality is about happiness and how one might have lived, not only rules and harms. She also points to debt-driven consumer culture as a structure that feeds the inner theater, and concludes that although grace is the surest aid, we owe one another a world where lust is difficult, built through the classics and embodied community.
points: Lust is defined as the reduction of our desire for communion into entertainment, a play in an inner theater with real casualties.
Augustine's concupiscence, fixation on pleasure itself, explains how experience becomes a windowless pocket where neither love nor understanding is possible.
Chekhov shows lust as a humble sin that can open into tenderness, while Flaubert shows the same impulse ending in ruin.
Hitz moves morality from rule-breaking and harm accounting to the question of how a person might have lived instead.
She names consumer debt culture and conformity as structures that dissipate eros and calls for a social world, not just personal discipline, that makes lust difficult.
quotes: Sexual desire has the odor of fate, thanks to its power to create illusions, delusions, and compulsions and to bestow, with apparent indifference, great happiness or deep misery.

Lust is the misuse of sexual desire. It has a subjective form—a desire to use another human being for one’s own pleasure—and an objective form, a desire that goes outside the bounds of good social order, one that cannot be integrated into the rest of a human life.

The capacity for human beings to trap themselves in the pleasures of mere experience was what Augustine called concupiscence. Our experiences give us pleasure; concupiscence draws us to fixate on the pleasure itself rather than the object or activity that bears it.
Concupiscence infuses every aspect of human experience, not just sexuality.
Lust in Chekhov’s story is a humble sin, worthy of pity. It causes no wars and burns no buildings.
Lust consists in the reduction of our desire for communion into a form of entertainment, a play in an inner theater, one where the actors take real blows and bleed real blood.

Our inherited conventional morality, such as it is, focuses on rules, rule-breaking, and acknowledged harm to individuals. Yet the sphere of morality is not that of law and punishment but that of happiness.
Our weaknesses are inborn, and for individuals, grace is the surest aid. Yet we surely owe one another a world where lust is difficult.
